extraction.body: President presses case for controversial $400m project following White House correspondents’ dinner shooting President presses case for controversial $400m project following White House correspondents’ dinner shooting The shooting at the Washington Hilton hotel gives new urgency to the project to construct a 1,000-seat ballroom at the White House, Donald Trump claimed after the incident on Saturday night. The US president pressed the case for his controversial ballroom initiative at the press conference he held at the White House on Saturday and a social media post on Sunday, after an armed attacker was arrested as he rushed towards the Hilton’s ballroom, where Trump was attending the White House Correspondents Association’s annual dinner . The $400m construction project to build a giant event space began at the White House with the East Wing being knocked down last October without Trump waiting for full legal permission to proceed. Legal challenges followed along with controversy over funding for the enormous ballroom, which is planned to be larger than the core White House itself. “What happened last night is exactly the reason that our great Military, Secret Service, Law Enforcement and, for different reasons, every President for the last 150 years, have been DEMANDING that a large, safe, and secure Ballroom be built ON THE GROUNDS OF THE WHITE HOUSE,” Trump posted on Truth Social on Sunday morning. He said that the shooting incident, which caused Trump and senior administration to be hustled out of the Hilton hotel complex, and hundreds of guests to duck for cover, “would never have happened with the Militarily Top Secret Ballroom currently under construction at the White House”. Trump pointed to existing security at the White House – “the most secure building in the world” – and “every highest level security feature there is” planned for the ballroom. “Plus, there are no rooms sitting on top for unsecured people to pour in,” he added, referring to the event taking place in a mainstream hotel. Trump’s comments were the second time in just over 12 hours that he mentioned the White House ballroom project in reference to the shooting incident. “I didn’t want to say this,” Trump said at a press briefing late Saturday after returning to the White House from the press dinner, “but this is why we have to have all of the attributes of what we’re planning at the White House. It’s actually a larger room, and it’s a much more secure. It’s got – it’s drone-proof, it’s bulletproof glass.” Trump has survived two previous assassination attempts, both during his 2024 election campaign. After the latest incident, Trump said in the White House briefing room that the scare would not affect the conduct of his life. “I like not to think about it,” he said. “I lead a pretty normal life, considering, you know, it’s a dangerous life. I think I’m, I think I handle it as well – as well as it can be handled. “To be honest with you, I’m not a basket case,” he added. But he also conceded that “it’s always shocking when something like this happens” and it had been “very unexpected”. He told Weijia Jiang, the CBS News correspondent and the president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, who was seated to his left at the dinner, that she had done “a fantastic job. What a beautiful evening.” Trump said he thought the noise that later turned out to be gunfire was “a tray going down. I’ve heard that many times, and it was a pretty loud noise, and it was from quite far away.” Melania Trump, he said, “was very cognizant, I think, of what happened. I think she knew immediately what happened. She was saying: ‘That’s a bad noise.’” Trump said it was “a rather traumatic experience for her”. Trump had been expected to roast the attending press corps during an after-dinner speech with what he said would have been the “most inappropriate speech ever made”. Even his being invited to the dinner was controversial after several years of calling the US media “the enemy of the people”. He has been repeatedly suing various media outlets, threatening broadcasters over their licenses and stepping up his attacks on some individual journalists when they ask him awkward questions. On Saturday night he suddenly now thanked the gathered journalists at the White House press briefing room, most still in the eveningwear they had donned for the dinner event. He praised “very responsible” coverage of the drama that had unfolded and said that when the press dinner is reorganized he is likely to give a different speech than the one he had planned for Saturday night. Then on Sunday, Trump said lawsuits seeking to stop the White House ballroom construction “must be dropped, immediately”, adding: “Nothing should be allowed to interfere with with its construction, which is on budget and substantially ahead of schedule.” That view was supported by at least one moderate Democrat, Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman. “That venue wasn’t built to accommodate an event with the line of succession for the US government,” Fetterman posted on X , referring to the Washington Hilton. “After witnessing last night, drop the TDS (‘Trump Derangement Syndrome’), and build the White House ballroom for events exactly like these,” he said.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump on Sunday assailed a federal judge’s injunction halting aboveground construction of the White House ballroom, emphasizing the enhanced security features that form a key part of the project. In a post on Truth Social, the president wrote that U.S. District Judge Richard Leon, a George W. Bush appointee, should “stop playing games with America’s Security.” Trump added an ominous warning that if anything were to happen, the judge “will be responsible for the Death and Destruction caused to our Country.” “He has already created enough problems by allowing ‘Top Secret’ information to be released and exposed based on a ridiculous lawsuit started by a highly litigious woman,” Trump noted. The National Trust for Historic Preservation filed a lawsuit in December to block the $400 million project, arguing that it cannot proceed until it receives congressional authorization. Leon agreed at the end of March, but that decision was later paused by a federal appeals court, allowing work to resume in the interim pending further review. The president invoked national security as a justification for forging ahead. His Sunday post featured two AI-generated renderings of military-style drones stationed on the rooftop and flanked by snipers. “The DronePort at the White House Ballroom will be, perhaps, the most sophisticated anywhere in the World! It will safeguard our Nation’s Capital, Washington, D.C., long into the future,” Trump said. “With the advent of highly sophisticated, and powerful, modern day weaponry, we can no longer defend Washington, D.C., with rifles and pistols, alone.” Trump hosted reporters for a tour of the site of the former East Wing in May, where he cast the development as both a ballroom and a fortress. Among the features he highlighted were a military hospital, missile-proof roofing and a “drone port” designed to accommodate an “unlimited number of drones.” “This is all my money and donors’ money. This is tax free,” Trump asserted. “On top of the roof, we’re going to have the greatest drone empire that you’ve ever seen and it’s going to protect Washington.” It remains unclear how or why drones would be deployed in this way. The specifics of security at the White House are not widely discussed but it has been reported that the building already has measures in place to combat potential drone attacks. Security in general is a significant concern, however. Over the past month, there have been three separate incidents in which gunfire erupted in close proximity to the president. On May 23, a gunman approached the White House while Trump was inside the residence, drew a firearm and discharged multiple rounds before being fatally shot by Secret Service agents. On May 4, a man was wounded during a firefight with Secret Service personnel near the Washington Monument. On April 25, an individual carrying a shotgun, handgun and knives attempted to breach a security checkpoint at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner — an event attended by the president — before being swiftly apprehended by law enforcement and charged with attempting to assassinate the president. The Justice Department is hoping the security imperatives will shape the trajectory of the legal dispute. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, in a court filing, insists it is “urgent” that the ballroom be completed. “This second attack on the President this month underscores that critical need for top level, state of the art security at the White House, including the Ballroom,” Blanche wrote in May, acknowledging that it is being constructed to “ensure that that President can perform his constitutional duties in a safe and heavily secured facility.” Tanya Noury is a reporter for Military Times and Defense News, with coverage focusing on the White House and Pentagon. The Pentagon remains mum about defense contractors’ plans to boost weapons production and delivery following a 21-day deadline for companies to send ideas. The newly established Homeland Defense Board aims to fill a gap Pentagon leaders see in providing military guidance to homeland security missions. extraction.body: WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal appeals court on Friday ordered President Donald Trump's administration to halt construction of its $400 million ballroom at the White House because the project lacks congressional approval. Trump doesn't have the unilateral authority to build a 90,000-square-foot (8,400-square-meter) ballroom where the White House's East Wing stood before he ordered its demolition last fall, according to the decision by a three-judge panel from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. The Republican president said in a post on social media that he would be appealing what he called an "unjust decision" to the U.S. Supreme Court. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Friday's ruling marked the second time this week the Trump administration has made headlines for construction plans that have been called into question. An assessment by the National Park Service found that a 250-foot-tall (76-meter-tall) triumphal arch that Trump has proposed building could compromise the historical significance of dozens of sites near its planned location on a traffic circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. In a 2-1 decision on the ballroom, the appeals court sided with historic preservationists who sued to stop construction of the massive structure, which has begun to rise aboveground on the east side of the White House, according to the most recent aerial photos of the site. The court said it would stay its ruling for two weeks to give the administration time to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court. "Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help," the court wrote. "This holding has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy. This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom. "What it does mean," the court continued, "is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court's expeditious litigation without securing Congress's authorization, as the Constitution and laws require." The president reacted to the ruling with a lengthy post on social media in which he quoted from a dissenting opinion issued by Judge Neomi Rao, whom he nominated. He also described the plans for the facility to include bomb shelters, a hospital and medical facilities, "Top Secret Military Facilities" and other security features. "The Military and Secret Service are viewing this horrendous, politically motivated, and unlawful ruling as a National Security threat to our Nation in that the entire Complex is being built for the protection of our Country and, additionally, all future Presidents," Trump wrote. After the lower court earlier this year ordered a halt to aboveground construction, the president argued that permission from Congress to build the ballroom was unnecessary because public money was not being used to pay for it. Trump has said he has raised hundreds of millions of dollars from corporations and wealthy people, including himself, to cover the construction costs. But the Trump administration requested $1 billion for the ballroom, which Congress refused in May. In June, Democrats warned that $350 million in funds from a tax cuts law appeared to have been redirected for the ballroom. WATCH: Trump calls planned White House ballroom 'a gift' to U.S. The National Trust for Historic Preservation, the nonprofit organization that brought the lawsuit against the Trump administration, said Friday's decision affirmed "the American people's right to voice their opinions about the historic places they cherish," including the White House. "From the beginning, our position has been clear and consistent: the law states that only Congress can authorize the construction of a ballroom at the White House," Brent Leggs, the group's president and CEO, said in a statement. "We are pleased with the DC Circuit Court's decision to uphold the District Court's preliminary injunction, which although stayed for 14 days will block any above-ground ballroom construction unless and until Congress takes action." The divided appeals court panel upheld an April 16 order from Leon for the Trump administration to halt aboveground work on the ballroom. Leon, who was nominated to the bench by Republican President George W. Bush, allowed construction to continue on underground work on a bunker and other "national security facilities" at the site. The appeals court case was assigned to Judges Rao, Patricia Millett and Bradley Garcia. Millett was nominated to the court by Democratic President Barack Obama. Garcia was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden. Both Millett and Garcia backed the decision, while Rao opposed it. The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued to challenge the project in December 2025, a week after completion of the East Wing demolition to make way for a ballroom that Trump says would hold 999 people. Government lawyers have argued that the project — the biggest structural change to the White House in more than 70 years — must move forward because it includes critical security features to guard against a range of threats, such as drones, ballistic missiles and biohazards. "These upgrades, alterations, and improvements are essential to protecting the President, his family, and his staff, as well as the White House itself, and the entire project flows from them," government attorneys wrote in a court filing. Attorneys for the preservation group countered that the lack of a White House ballroom doesn't constitute a national security emergency. "That commonsense conclusion is not clearly erroneous, and there is no basis to disturb it," they wrote. In an initial ruling that the government also appealed, Leon barred aboveground work on the ballroom from proceeding without congressional approval. In response, the appeals court instructed the judge to reconsider the national security implications of stopping construction. In his most recent decision, Leon ordered a stop only to the aboveground construction of the planned ballroom. The judge stressed that the White House is free to proceed with underground work, including the construction of any bunkers, military installations and medical facilities. On April 2, Trump's ballroom won final approval from the 12-member National Capital Planning Commission, which is charged with approving construction on federal property in the Washington region. Associated Press writers Bill Barrow in Atlanta and Gary Fields and Michelle L. Price in Washington contributed to this report. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Left: Construction of a ballroom at the White House seen from a window at the Washington Monument, in Washington, D.C., on Aug. 4, 2026. Photo by Eric Lee/Reuters

In February, the president announced in a Truth Social post that the Trump Kennedy Center will close for a two-year renovation. The monument, a near twin of Paris’ iconic Arc de Triomphe, is meant to welcome visitors crossing the Memorial Bridge from Arlington National Cemetery into the heart of the nation’s capital. extraction.body: President presses case for controversial $400m project following White House correspondents’ dinner shooting President presses case for controversial $400m project following White House correspondents’ dinner shooting The shooting at the Washington Hilton hotel gives new urgency to the project to construct a 1,000-seat ballroom at the White House, Donald Trump claimed after the incident on Saturday night. The US president pressed the case for his controversial ballroom initiative at the press conference he held at the White House on Saturday and a social media post on Sunday, after an armed attacker was arrested as he rushed towards the Hilton’s ballroom, where Trump was attending the White House Correspondents Association’s annual dinner . The $400m construction project to build a giant event space began at the White House with the East Wing being knocked down last October without Trump waiting for full legal permission to proceed. Legal challenges followed along with controversy over funding for the enormous ballroom, which is planned to be larger than the core White House itself. “What happened last night is exactly the reason that our great Military, Secret Service, Law Enforcement and, for different reasons, every President for the last 150 years, have been DEMANDING that a large, safe, and secure Ballroom be built ON THE GROUNDS OF THE WHITE HOUSE,” Trump posted on Truth Social on Sunday morning. He said that the shooting incident, which caused Trump and senior administration to be hustled out of the Hilton hotel complex, and hundreds of guests to duck for cover, “would never have happened with the Militarily Top Secret Ballroom currently under construction at the White House”. Trump pointed to existing security at the White House – “the most secure building in the world” – and “every highest level security feature there is” planned for the ballroom. “Plus, there are no rooms sitting on top for unsecured people to pour in,” he added, referring to the event taking place in a mainstream hotel. Trump’s comments were the second time in just over 12 hours that he mentioned the White House ballroom project in reference to the shooting incident. “I didn’t want to say this,” Trump said at a press briefing late Saturday after returning to the White House from the press dinner, “but this is why we have to have all of the attributes of what we’re planning at the White House. It’s actually a larger room, and it’s a much more secure. It’s got – it’s drone-proof, it’s bulletproof glass.” Trump has survived two previous assassination attempts, both during his 2024 election campaign. After the latest incident, Trump said in the White House briefing room that the scare would not affect the conduct of his life. “I like not to think about it,” he said. “I lead a pretty normal life, considering, you know, it’s a dangerous life. I think I’m, I think I handle it as well – as well as it can be handled. “To be honest with you, I’m not a basket case,” he added. But he also conceded that “it’s always shocking when something like this happens” and it had been “very unexpected”. He told Weijia Jiang, the CBS News correspondent and the president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, who was seated to his left at the dinner, that she had done “a fantastic job. What a beautiful evening.” Trump said he thought the noise that later turned out to be gunfire was “a tray going down. I’ve heard that many times, and it was a pretty loud noise, and it was from quite far away.” Melania Trump, he said, “was very cognizant, I think, of what happened. I think she knew immediately what happened. She was saying: ‘That’s a bad noise.’” Trump said it was “a rather traumatic experience for her”. Trump had been expected to roast the attending press corps during an after-dinner speech with what he said would have been the “most inappropriate speech ever made”. Even his being invited to the dinner was controversial after several years of calling the US media “the enemy of the people”. He has been repeatedly suing various media outlets, threatening broadcasters over their licenses and stepping up his attacks on some individual journalists when they ask him awkward questions. On Saturday night he suddenly now thanked the gathered journalists at the White House press briefing room, most still in the eveningwear they had donned for the dinner event. He praised “very responsible” coverage of the drama that had unfolded and said that when the press dinner is reorganized he is likely to give a different speech than the one he had planned for Saturday night. Then on Sunday, Trump said lawsuits seeking to stop the White House ballroom construction “must be dropped, immediately”, adding: “Nothing should be allowed to interfere with with its construction, which is on budget and substantially ahead of schedule.” That view was supported by at least one moderate Democrat, Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman. “That venue wasn’t built to accommodate an event with the line of succession for the US government,” Fetterman posted on X , referring to the Washington Hilton. “After witnessing last night, drop the TDS (‘Trump Derangement Syndrome’), and build the White House ballroom for events exactly like these,” he said.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal appeals court on Friday ordered President Donald Trump's administration to halt construction of its $400 million ballroom at the White House because the project lacks congressional approval. Trump doesn't have the unilateral authority to build a 90,000-square-foot (8,400-square-meter) ballroom where the White House's East Wing stood before he ordered its demolition last fall, according to the decision by a three-judge panel from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. The Republican president said in a post on social media that he would be appealing what he called an "unjust decision" to the U.S. Supreme Court. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Friday's ruling marked the second time this week the Trump administration has made headlines for construction plans that have been called into question. An assessment by the National Park Service found that a 250-foot-tall (76-meter-tall) triumphal arch that Trump has proposed building could compromise the historical significance of dozens of sites near its planned location on a traffic circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. In a 2-1 decision on the ballroom, the appeals court sided with historic preservationists who sued to stop construction of the massive structure, which has begun to rise aboveground on the east side of the White House, according to the most recent aerial photos of the site. The court said it would stay its ruling for two weeks to give the administration time to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court. "Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help," the court wrote. "This holding has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy. This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom. "What it does mean," the court continued, "is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court's expeditious litigation without securing Congress's authorization, as the Constitution and laws require." The president reacted to the ruling with a lengthy post on social media in which he quoted from a dissenting opinion issued by Judge Neomi Rao, whom he nominated. He also described the plans for the facility to include bomb shelters, a hospital and medical facilities, "Top Secret Military Facilities" and other security features. "The Military and Secret Service are viewing this horrendous, politically motivated, and unlawful ruling as a National Security threat to our Nation in that the entire Complex is being built for the protection of our Country and, additionally, all future Presidents," Trump wrote. After the lower court earlier this year ordered a halt to aboveground construction, the president argued that permission from Congress to build the ballroom was unnecessary because public money was not being used to pay for it. Trump has said he has raised hundreds of millions of dollars from corporations and wealthy people, including himself, to cover the construction costs. But the Trump administration requested $1 billion for the ballroom, which Congress refused in May. In June, Democrats warned that $350 million in funds from a tax cuts law appeared to have been redirected for the ballroom. WATCH: Trump calls planned White House ballroom 'a gift' to U.S. The National Trust for Historic Preservation, the nonprofit organization that brought the lawsuit against the Trump administration, said Friday's decision affirmed "the American people's right to voice their opinions about the historic places they cherish," including the White House. "From the beginning, our position has been clear and consistent: the law states that only Congress can authorize the construction of a ballroom at the White House," Brent Leggs, the group's president and CEO, said in a statement. "We are pleased with the DC Circuit Court's decision to uphold the District Court's preliminary injunction, which although stayed for 14 days will block any above-ground ballroom construction unless and until Congress takes action." The divided appeals court panel upheld an April 16 order from Leon for the Trump administration to halt aboveground work on the ballroom. Leon, who was nominated to the bench by Republican President George W. Bush, allowed construction to continue on underground work on a bunker and other "national security facilities" at the site. The appeals court case was assigned to Judges Rao, Patricia Millett and Bradley Garcia. Millett was nominated to the court by Democratic President Barack Obama. Garcia was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden. Both Millett and Garcia backed the decision, while Rao opposed it. The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued to challenge the project in December 2025, a week after completion of the East Wing demolition to make way for a ballroom that Trump says would hold 999 people. Government lawyers have argued that the project — the biggest structural change to the White House in more than 70 years — must move forward because it includes critical security features to guard against a range of threats, such as drones, ballistic missiles and biohazards. "These upgrades, alterations, and improvements are essential to protecting the President, his family, and his staff, as well as the White House itself, and the entire project flows from them," government attorneys wrote in a court filing. Attorneys for the preservation group countered that the lack of a White House ballroom doesn't constitute a national security emergency. "That commonsense conclusion is not clearly erroneous, and there is no basis to disturb it," they wrote. In an initial ruling that the government also appealed, Leon barred aboveground work on the ballroom from proceeding without congressional approval. In response, the appeals court instructed the judge to reconsider the national security implications of stopping construction. In his most recent decision, Leon ordered a stop only to the aboveground construction of the planned ballroom. The judge stressed that the White House is free to proceed with underground work, including the construction of any bunkers, military installations and medical facilities. On April 2, Trump's ballroom won final approval from the 12-member National Capital Planning Commission, which is charged with approving construction on federal property in the Washington region. Associated Press writers Bill Barrow in Atlanta and Gary Fields and Michelle L. Price in Washington contributed to this report. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. If you live in the US and purchased an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or any iPhone 16 model between June 10th, 2024, and March 29th, 2025, you can file a claim on the settlement’s website, as reported earlier by MacRumors. Instead, the iPhone 16 launched with a more limited set of capabilities despite being labeled as “built for Apple Intelligence.” The company later delayed the rollout of its AI-upgraded Siri, which only just arrived with iOS 27 earlier this month.

passages: The Apple Intelligence settlement is separate from an earlier $95 million Siri privacy settlement , which involved allegations about unintended Siri activations and recordings.
The new $250 million agreement concerns marketing claims tied to Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features on recent iPhone models, not the older privacy case.

Apple has agreed to pay $250 million to settle a proposed class-action lawsuit accusing the company of misleading consumers about artificial intelligence features promoted for Siri and the iPhone 16 lineup, according to court filings and statements from attorneys involved in the case.

Cotchett, Pitre & McCarthy, one of the firms representing the proposed class, said the settlement would apply to U.S. consumers and businesses that bought eligible iPhones during the class period and submit valid claims, while emphasizing that Apple does not admit liability under the agreement.
District Court for the Northern District of California and centers on Apple’s marketing of “Apple Intelligence,” including promised upgrades to Siri.

In Apple’s case, plaintiffs alleged that the promise of a more capable Siri was a key part of the company’s iPhone marketing campaign, and that buyers would not have purchased the devices, or would have paid less, had they known the features were delayed.

Apple said in a statement reported by The Associated Press that it reached the settlement to resolve claims related to the availability of two additional features, adding that it wanted to stay focused on delivering products and services to users.
The settlement has not yet received final court approval, and Apple has denied wrongdoing.
Court filings state that no portion of the total settlement fund would revert to Apple .
Eligible customers will not receive payment automatically unless they submit a valid claim.

Potential class members should wait for official notice from the settlement administrator, confirm their device model and purchase date, and avoid unofficial claim links or sites that are not referenced in court-approved notices.

extraction.body: Shares of U.S.-listed companies exposed to Greenland surged on Monday after the U.S. and Denmark reached a deal on security arrangements on the Arctic territory. Shares of Greenland Energy soared 159%, with Greenland Mines seen up more than 200% and Critical Metals Corp nearly 37% higher. The agreement, which is expected to be signed during the United Nations General Assembly this week, will see the U.S., Denmark and Greenland enter into a pact to develop a significant military presence on the territory, while blocking Washington's adversaries from building their own bases there. It follows several months of U.S. President Donald Trum p's threats to annex the self-governing Danish territory, with the president insisting Greenland is critical to U.S. national security. Announcing the deal, Trump said via Truth Social on Friday that the U.S. would "FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America." Trump said the agreement would come at no cost to the U.S., adding that Washington would "immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many." Key details of the agreement have not yet been made public. Greenlandic and Danish officials sought to reassure citizens over the weekend that the deal would respect the island's right to self-determination and the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom. "It is joyous that we are about to make an agreement that will ensure and strengthen the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western Alliance," Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a statement. "The agreement recognizes Greenland's interests and our place in the international cooperation. It is to the benefit of us all," he added. Greenland Energy is an oil and gas exploration firm focused on trying to unlock the hydrocarbon potential of the Jameson Land Basin on the island's east coast. The Texas-based company, which has links to Trump , recently delayed plans to drill for oil in Greenland after the island's government issued a " strong warning " to its joint venture partner for bringing equipment ashore without permission. Greenland Mines, meanwhile, is a natural resources company working on the Skaergaard Project, which ranks among the world's largest undeveloped palladium, gold and platinum deposits. The rally followed a U.S.-Denmark-Greenland security pact aimed at expanding the military presence on the Arctic territory. Stocks of U.S.-listed companies with operational ties to Greenland experienced significant gains on Monday following the announcement of a new security agreement between the United States, Denmark, and Greenland. The trilateral pact, announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, aims to substantially expand the American military presence in the strategically vital Arctic territory. The market reaction was immediate and forceful across the basic materials sector. Shares of Greenland Energy (GLND) jumped 119 percent in extended trading, while Greenland Mines (GGRML) rose 58 percent. Critical Metals Corp (CRML) also saw a 20 percent increase. The surge reflects intense investor anticipation that the military agreement will pave the way for increased U.S. infrastructure investment and financial support for resource extraction in the region. While the diplomatic arrangement focuses explicitly on defense and preventing geopolitical adversaries from establishing Arctic bases, private capital is aggressively pricing in the secondary economic benefits of a reinforced American security umbrella. The pact is expected to be formally signed later this week during the United Nations General Assembly in New York. The new security arrangement places Arctic access at the center of U.S. foreign policy. Historically, the United States has maintained a critical strategic foothold in Greenland through the Thule Air Base—recently renamed Pituffik Space Base—which operates early warning radar systems essential for North American aerospace defense. The new pact is designed to expand this presence, allowing for greater troop deployments, maritime coordination, and shared intelligence operations. For the defense infrastructure to function effectively in the harsh Arctic environment, significant logistical upgrades are required. Military expansion inherently demands improved deep-water ports, reinforced airstrips, and robust telecommunications networks. It is this anticipated dual-use infrastructure that has galvanized the equity markets, as mining and energy companies operating in Greenland frequently cite severe logistical bottlenecks as their primary operational constraint. The agreement emerges against a backdrop of escalating geopolitical competition. As the polar ice caps retreat, new shipping routes are opening, and the race to secure access to the Arctic seabed has intensified. Both Russia and China have expressed strong strategic interest in the region, prompting Washington to solidify its alliances with Copenhagen and the semi-autonomous government in Nuuk. The dramatic rise in Greenland-linked equities highlights the speculative nature of frontier market investing. The current surge draws direct comparisons to August 2019 and earlier in 2026, when President Trump publicly floated the idea of the United States purchasing Greenland outright. While those proposals were swiftly rejected by Danish and Greenlandic officials, they successfully signaled to the market that Washington views the island as a paramount national security interest. However, analysts caution that the current rally is built heavily on projection rather than immediate commercial reality. The security pact announced on Monday did not include specific commercial funding, fast-tracked mining permits, or direct subsidies for the resource sector. Companies like Greenland Mines and Critical Metals remain in the exploratory or early developmental stages, facing immense environmental and regulatory hurdles before they can achieve commercial production. The primary economic draw of Greenland lies in its vast, largely untapped deposits of rare earth elements, uranium, and base metals. These materials are critical for the global energy transition, powering everything from electric vehicle batteries to advanced military guidance systems. Currently, global supply chains for rare earth elements are heavily dominated by China, creating an urgent accountability mandate for Western governments to secure independent supply lines. By expanding its military footprint, the U.S. government is effectively de-risking the jurisdiction for private capital. However, the ultimate authority over resource extraction resides with the Greenlandic government in Nuuk. Local authorities must balance the promise of economic independence—fueled by mining royalties—with profound environmental concerns and the preservation of traditional Indigenous ways of life. The intersection of military expansion and speculative mining carries profound implications for Greenland's population of roughly 56,000 people. While the influx of American capital could provide the economic foundation necessary for Greenland to pursue full independence from Denmark, it also risks overwhelming local institutions. The rapid industrialization of pristine Arctic environments remains a highly contentious domestic political issue. For the companies whose stocks surged this week, the challenge will be translating geopolitical momentum into operational success. The harsh climate, lack of existing infrastructure, and stringent environmental regulations mean that establishing a profitable mine in Greenland requires billions of dollars in upfront capital and years of patient development. Investors and policy analysts are now looking toward the United Nations General Assembly, where the formal signing of the pact is expected to yield specific details regarding troop deployments and infrastructure commitments. The ultimate test of Monday's market rally will be whether the U.S. government follows its military agreements with concrete financial mechanisms, such as Export-Import Bank financing, to support the commercial ambitions of the surging equities. Companies like Greenland Mines and Critical Metals remain in the exploratory or early developmental stages, facing immense environmental and regulatory hurdles before they can achieve commercial production.

The primary economic draw of Greenland lies in its vast, largely untapped deposits of rare earth elements, uranium, and base metals. These materials are critical for the global energy transition, powering everything from electric vehicle batteries to advanced military guidance systems. Currently, global supply chains for rare earth elements are heavily dominated by China, creating an urgent accountability mandate for Western governments to secure independent supply lines.

By expanding its military footprint, the U.S. government is effectively de-risking the jurisdiction for private capital. However, the ultimate authority over resource extraction resides with the Greenlandic government in Nuuk. Local authorities must balance the promise of economic independence—fueled by mining royalties—with profound environmental concerns and the preservation of traditional Indigenous ways of life.

The intersection of military expansion and speculative mining carries profound implications for Greenland's population of roughly 56,000 people. While the influx of American capital could provide the economic foundation necessary for Greenland to pursue full independence from Denmark, it also risks overwhelming local institutions. The rapid industrialization of pristine Arctic environments remains a highly contentious domestic political issue.

For the companies whose stocks surged this week, the challenge will be translating geopolitical momentum into operational success. The harsh climate, lack of existing infrastructure, and stringent environmental regulations mean that establishing a profitable mine in Greenland requires billions of dollars in upfront capital and years of patient development.

Investors and policy analysts are now looking toward the United Nations General Assembly, where the formal signing of the pact is expected to yield specific details regarding troop deployments and infrastructure commitments. The ultimate test of Monday's market rally will be whether the U.S. government follows its military agreements with concrete financial mechanisms, such as Export-Import Bank financing, to support the commercial ambitions of the surging equities.

sources.title: Trump’s Greenland deal: How Arctic pact bolsters Golden Dome against Russia, China
passages: Trump announces agreement with Denmark to secure ‘permanent’ control over Greenland’s security.Why Greenland matters for the Golden DomeGolden Dome is Trump’s proposed multi-layered missile defence system designed to detect, track and intercept ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles targeting the US.

We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many,' Trump wrote while annoucing the deal.What has actually been agreedDanish prime minister Mette Frederiksen said the deal does not hand the United States sovereignty over Greenland, describing it instead an arrangement that strengthens shared security in the Arctic and North Atlantic and recognises the Greenlandic people's right to self determination.The United States, Denmark and Greenland are expected to sign the text next week at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, reported CNBC.

It has also been point out that interceptor tests over the past two decades have succeeded only about half the time, and under conditions far kinder than a real attack.Locking out Moscow and BeijingThe second purpose of the deal is to keep rivals out as Trump said no American adversary may ever build a base in Greenland, station forces there, or make sensitive investments, without express written approval from Washington.In plain terms, a Chinese state firm buying a stake in a Greenlandic mine or port would now need an American signature first.

Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule, lies above the Arctic Circle roughly halfway between Washington and Moscow, and its radar can watch deep into Russia and across the likely flight paths of Chinese missiles, buying American decision makers precious extra minutes.Trump wants Golden Dome fully working by January 2029 at a cost of 175 billion dollars, a timetable and price tag that seems doubtful.
The official wording had not been released when Trump made his announcement.
The Tanbreez project in southern Greenland, now 92.5 per cent owned by Nasdaq listed Critical Metals, is the furthest along, with full construction not expected before spring 2027.

The rally followed a U.S.-Denmark-Greenland security pact aimed at expanding the military presence on the Arctic territory. Stocks of U.S.-listed companies with operational ties to Greenland experienced significant gains on Monday following the announcement of a new security agreement between the United States, Denmark, and Greenland. The trilateral pact, announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, aims to substantially expand the American military presence in the strategically vital Arctic territory. The market reaction was immediate and forceful across the basic materials sector. Shares of Greenland Energy (GLND) jumped 119 percent in extended trading, while Greenland Mines (GGRML) rose 58 percent. Critical Metals Corp (CRML) also saw a 20 percent increase. The surge reflects intense investor anticipation that the military agreement will pave the way for increased U.S. infrastructure investment and financial support for resource extraction in the region. While the diplomatic arrangement focuses explicitly on defense and preventing geopolitical adversaries from establishing Arctic bases, private capital is aggressively pricing in the secondary economic benefits of a reinforced American security umbrella. The pact is expected to be formally signed later this week during the United Nations General Assembly in New York. The new security arrangement places Arctic access at the center of U.S. foreign policy. Historically, the United States has maintained a critical strategic foothold in Greenland through the Thule Air Base—recently renamed Pituffik Space Base—which operates early warning radar systems essential for North American aerospace defense. The new pact is designed to expand this presence, allowing for greater troop deployments, maritime coordination, and shared intelligence operations. For the defense infrastructure to function effectively in the harsh Arctic environment, significant logistical upgrades are required. Military expansion inherently demands improved deep-water ports, reinforced airstrips, and robust telecommunications networks. It is this anticipated dual-use infrastructure that has galvanized the equity markets, as mining and energy companies operating in Greenland frequently cite severe logistical bottlenecks as their primary operational constraint. The agreement emerges against a backdrop of escalating geopolitical competition. As the polar ice caps retreat, new shipping routes are opening, and the race to secure access to the Arctic seabed has intensified. Both Russia and China have expressed strong strategic interest in the region, prompting Washington to solidify its alliances with Copenhagen and the semi-autonomous government in Nuuk. The dramatic rise in Greenland-linked equities highlights the speculative nature of frontier market investing. The current surge draws direct comparisons to August 2019 and earlier in 2026, when President Trump publicly floated the idea of the United States purchasing Greenland outright. While those proposals were swiftly rejected by Danish and Greenlandic officials, they successfully signaled to the market that Washington views the island as a paramount national security interest. However, analysts caution that the current rally is built heavily on projection rather than immediate commercial reality. The security pact announced on Monday did not include specific commercial funding, fast-tracked mining permits, or direct subsidies for the resource sector. Companies like Greenland Mines and Critical Metals remain in the exploratory or early developmental stages, facing immense environmental and regulatory hurdles before they can achieve commercial production. The primary economic draw of Greenland lies in its vast, largely untapped deposits of rare earth elements, uranium, and base metals. These materials are critical for the global energy transition, powering everything from electric vehicle batteries to advanced military guidance systems. Currently, global supply chains for rare earth elements are heavily dominated by China, creating an urgent accountability mandate for Western governments to secure independent supply lines. By expanding its military footprint, the U.S. government is effectively de-risking the jurisdiction for private capital. However, the ultimate authority over resource extraction resides with the Greenlandic government in Nuuk. Local authorities must balance the promise of economic independence—fueled by mining royalties—with profound environmental concerns and the preservation of traditional Indigenous ways of life. The intersection of military expansion and speculative mining carries profound implications for Greenland's population of roughly 56,000 people. While the influx of American capital could provide the economic foundation necessary for Greenland to pursue full independence from Denmark, it also risks overwhelming local institutions. The rapid industrialization of pristine Arctic environments remains a highly contentious domestic political issue. For the companies whose stocks surged this week, the challenge will be translating geopolitical momentum into operational success. The harsh climate, lack of existing infrastructure, and stringent environmental regulations mean that establishing a profitable mine in Greenland requires billions of dollars in upfront capital and years of patient development. Investors and policy analysts are now looking toward the United Nations General Assembly, where the formal signing of the pact is expected to yield specific details regarding troop deployments and infrastructure commitments. The ultimate test of Monday's market rally will be whether the U.S. government follows its military agreements with concrete financial mechanisms, such as Export-Import Bank financing, to support the commercial ambitions of the surging equities. Trump called it an agreement with no end and said it would come at no cost to the United States.'This is an “Infinite Life” Agreement, there is no end! We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many,' Trump wrote while annoucing the deal.What has actually been agreedDanish prime minister Mette Frederiksen said the deal does not hand the United States sovereignty over Greenland, describing it instead an arrangement that strengthens shared security in the Arctic and North Atlantic and recognises the Greenlandic people's right to self determination.The United States, Denmark and Greenland are expected to sign the text next week at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, reported CNBC. The official wording had not been released when Trump made his announcement. Trump announces agreement with Denmark to secure ‘permanent’ control over Greenland’s security.Why Greenland matters for the Golden DomeGolden Dome is Trump’s proposed multi-layered missile defence system designed to detect, track and intercept ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles targeting the US. Greenland matters because of its location in the Arctic, particularly for monitoring missile activity from Russia and supporting early-warning capabilities.Greater US access to Greenland could therefore strengthen the Arctic component of Golden Dome, while limiting potential military or strategic access for China and Russia.The shortest route for a missile fired from Russia towards American cities runs over the North Pole, and Greenland sits almost exactly underneath that path. Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule, lies above the Arctic Circle roughly halfway between Washington and Moscow, and its radar can watch deep into Russia and across the likely flight paths of Chinese missiles, buying American decision makers precious extra minutes.Trump wants Golden Dome fully working by January 2029 at a cost of 175 billion dollars, a timetable and price tag that seems doubtful. It has also been point out that interceptor tests over the past two decades have succeeded only about half the time, and under conditions far kinder than a real attack.Locking out Moscow and BeijingThe second purpose of the deal is to keep rivals out as Trump said no American adversary may ever build a base in Greenland, station forces there, or make sensitive investments, without express written approval from Washington.In plain terms, a Chinese state firm buying a stake in a Greenlandic mine or port would now need an American signature first. That single clause is aimed squarely at the quiet economic route into the Arctic that Beijing has used elsewhere.Moscow has already bristled at the idea, with Russian officials calling Golden Dome provocative and warned of military and technical countermeasures if American missile systems appear on the island.Greenland is also a mineral prize as official Danish and Greenlandic geological surveys estimate the island holds some 36 million tonnes of rare earth resources, alongside graphite, copper, nickel, zinc and tungsten, and it hosts deposits of 25 of the 34 raw materials the European Commission treats as critical. The Tanbreez project in southern Greenland, now 92.5 per cent owned by Nasdaq listed Critical Metals, is the furthest along, with full construction not expected before spring 2027.

It was new Apple CEO John Ternus’ first major product launch since he took over for former CEO Tim Cook less than two weeks prior.
This year’s story actually says a great deal about what’s happening at Apple, how Cook managed in wholesale leadership ranks over the past year, and how all of that might change Apple’s culture.

extraction.body: Today, I’m talking with Mark Gurman, who is the world’s best-sourced Apple reporter — both as Bloomberg’s chief Apple correspondent and the host of the upcoming podcast Power On. Earlier this month, Apple hosted its annual iPhone hardware event, virtually every detail of which was reported ahead of time by Mark. It was new Apple CEO John Ternus’ first major product launch since he took over for former CEO Tim Cook less than two weeks prior. It was also the debut of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable smartphone. Apple takes these hardware events — and the stories they tell — extremely seriously. This year’s story actually says a great deal about what’s happening at Apple, how Cook managed in wholesale leadership ranks over the past year, and how all of that might change Apple’s culture. Furthermore, what all that tells about Ternus’ plan to navigate Apple from what you might call the iPhone era into the AI era. Okay: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman on the future of Apple. Mark Gurman, you’re the chief Apple correspondent and the managing editor of consumer technology at Bloomberg. And it’s been a while, so it’s good to catch up on all things Apple. This is a Decoder episode, so we’ve got a new CEO, and we’ve got a new org chart inside of Apple. The thing with me, and I don’t know if most people know this about me, but I hope people know this about me, is that I’m a huge Apple fan through and through, and I’ve always been. And I’m so lucky to be able to cover a company that I love, a company that I am obsessed with, and a company whose products I use. So I do what I do because I love Apple and I love covering Apple. You got your start as an Apple blogger at the Apple rumor sites. There’s a whole culture around Apple that has grown up and changed over the years, and you can trace it to different eras of hardware, to different CEOs, to different sizes of the company. This was the first event with John Ternus as CEO. Apple announced a big new product in the iPhone Duo. And do you think Ternus is going to lead to a difference in what that community feels like? It could have been Ternus up there introducing it. The one thing I will say that did feel slightly different is that Ternus came out swinging with a point of view on AI. The first thing he came out with was about the intelligent personal hub. Now, here’s the big difference between Tim Cook and John Ternus in terms of their management style. You’re inside Apple, you’re an executive, you’ll come to him with an idea, you’ll come to him with a viewpoint, a decision, an opinion, and he’ll just pepper you with more questions. John Ternus, if you come to him and you want him to make a decision, he’ll make a decision. But that’s the big difference between talking to people about Ternus and Tim. Ternus comes out talking about his view on AI. Apple’s been at this AI game now for two years since they launched Apple Intelligence at WWDC in 2024, and it’s been a mishmash of things. So, as I said, whether you agree with it or not, they did do that. All right, we’re just going to get into the weeds of Apple nerds disagreeing about things. I sat through that event, and I appreciated the same thing that you saw, which is, “Oh, we’re telling a story.” John Ternus is on the stage, and the first thing he’s doing is telling a story about this product and how it fits into the universe of technology. And then I took a beat, and I was like, oh, but they’re also just making sure that he’s successful at his first event by playing Apple’s greatest hits. Because an “intelligent personal hub” is just a replay of Steve Jobs saying the iMac was the digital hub. At the very end of the event, Ternus said, “There’s one more thing, and it’s the iPhone Duo.” There was just a part of all of that that, to me, felt like Apple saying, “Look, our new CEO can put on the clothes of the old CEO. It’s the same week that Meta launched Muse, right? I just felt like there was a part where they were playing it really safe with John by having him basically show up and be the new lead singer of Journey.

sources.title: Apple’s New CEO Needs To Find Its Next iPhone: ‘That’s Ternus’s Big Job,’ Says Futurum Group CEO - TradingView
passages: Apple (AAPL) needs to find its next iPhone, and that will be incoming CEO John Ternus’s biggest challenge, according to Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman.
Ternus takes over as Apple CEO on Tuesday, succeeding Tim Cook after more than a decade at the helm.
Newman said Ternus faces an immediate question over Apple's AI strategy, particularly the company's efforts to improve Siri.
However, he stated the bigger issue is whether Apple can identify and lead the next major computing platform after the smartphone.
Apple’s Next CEO Faces The Post-iPhone Question
“I think Apple needs to own this,” Newman said in a CNBC interview, referring to the next generation of computing devices.
According to Newman, Cook built a global supply chain and what he described as some of the strongest unit economics in tech.
He added that Ternus brings a different skill set, having risen through Apple’s hardware and engineering ranks, which also leaves him with “some big shoes to fill.”
Newman pointed to OpenAI and Meta as companies working on new devices that could change how consumers interact with technology.
If those products gain traction, Apple could find itself defending its existing hardware ecosystem rather than defining the next one.
On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the iPhone maker fell to ‘extremely bearish’ from ‘bearish’ territory over the past day.
Retail investors are also looking to Ternus to bring a change in Apple's product strategy.
AAPL stock has gained over 2,200% under Cook’s tenure, but underperformed peers.
One Stocktwits user believes that Cook's departure could pave the way for a new iPhone design, while another said that the first big test comes at Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event.
According to him, the problem is that Apple has yet to fully capitalize on that position.
Siri has not developed into the AI assistant many users expected, while Apple's other attempts to establish new product categories have also produced limited results.
Newman noted that people increasingly experience services such as Claude and ChatGPT through Apple devices, particularly the iPhone.
“The device of the future, we know OpenAI is trying to develop stuff.

sources.title: Who is John Ternus? Apple’s new CEO takes charge ahead of iPhone 18 launch - Convergence Now
passages: John Ternus will become Apple’s new CEO on September 1, replacing Tim Cook after 15 years.
His first major test will come just eight days later, when Apple is expected to unveil its next iPhone generation and potentially its first foldable iPhone.
John Ternus is an engineer who has spent most of his career at Apple.
He joined the company in 2001 and rose through its hardware organisation.
He has worked on major Apple products, including the iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple Watch.
In 2021, he became Apple’s senior vice president of Hardware Engineering.
The iPhone remains central to Apple’s business, but the company needs to find products that can create new growth.
Apple has expanded into services, wearables and mixed-reality hardware, including the Vision Pro.
However, none has yet matched the commercial impact of the iPhone.
That puts greater attention on what comes next.
Before joining Apple, Ternus worked as a mechanical engineer at Virtual Research Systems.
He studied mechanical engineering at the University of Pennsylvania.
His appointment also marks a change in the type of leadership at Apple.
Cook was closely associated with Apple’s operations, supply chain, manufacturing and global business.
Ternus comes from the product and engineering side of the company.
Apple’s board has described Ternus as a leader with deep technical knowledge and a strong focus on product development.
Reports have pointed to a broader product pipeline that could eventually include smart home devices, a tabletop robot, camera-equipped AirPods, smart glasses and other new products.
Apple’s challenge will therefore be bigger than simply producing a foldable handset.
It will need to convince consumers that its approach offers enough value to make the technology mainstream.
The launch could also show whether Ternus intends to push Apple towards more ambitious hardware products.
Apple has confirmed a major product event for September 9.
The event will be the first major Apple launch under Ternus, who will have been CEO for just over a week.
A foldable iPhone is also widely expected, although Apple has not officially confirmed the product.
But hardware alone will not determine his success.
Apple said the CEO transition was part of a long-term succession plan and was unanimously approved by its board.
Cook became Apple CEO in 2011, following the final months of Steve Jobs’ leadership.
During his tenure, Apple expanded its product portfolio and services business while becoming increasingly reliant on a complex global supply chain.
Ternus now inherits that entire operation, but with a different set of challenges.
Artificial intelligence is likely to be one of Ternus’ biggest challenges.
Apple introduced Siri in 2011, but the rise of generative AI has changed the technology landscape.
Companies such as Google, OpenAI and Microsoft have moved quickly with AI assistants, agents and large language models.
Apple, meanwhile, has faced delays in delivering some of its more ambitious Siri upgrades.
The challenge for Ternus is not simply to add more AI features to Apple products.
That matters because Apple’s traditional strength has been the close integration of its hardware, software and services.
At the same time, tensions between the US and China, tariffs, export restrictions and Beijing’s push for domestic technology have created additional risks.
Apple has been expanding production in countries such as India and Vietnam, but moving its entire manufacturing ecosystem away from China is not a simple task.
These specifications remain based on reports and leaks rather than Apple’s official announcement.
If Apple does launch the device, it will enter a category where Samsung and other manufacturers have already spent years developing foldable phones.
That may ultimately be Ternus’ biggest challenge.
The foldable iPhone, if launched as expected, could give Ternus an opportunity to demonstrate that Apple can still enter a new category and influence the market.
Apple also faces a difficult supply-chain challenge.
China remains an important part of Apple’s manufacturing network, with a large ecosystem of suppliers, component makers, skilled workers and production facilities.
If key AI capabilities increasingly come from external companies, Apple could lose some of that control.
The bigger question is: Can Apple build an AI ecosystem that is as influential as the iPhone?
The leadership change comes at a crucial time for Apple.

sources.title: What to expect from Apple’s next big event - including new iPhone software and (finally) a revamped Siri - stuff.tv
passages: Apple is set to hold its annual developer conference next week and, as always, there will be a lot to talk about, including new software for the iPhone , iPad and Apple Watch.
Not only is it CEO Tim Cook’s last outing before he is replaced by John Ternus on 1 September, but it is another big event from Apple’s 50th anniversary year .
As usual we’ll get new software previews for all of Apple’s operating systems, including iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, visionOS 27 and tvOS 27.
I presume the naming convention will follow that of last year’s given this is only the second year the new ‘year-by-year’ nomenclature will have been used.
As usual, this software will be available for developers straight away, with a public beta to follow at a later date.
The final software will then launch in the fall.
Expect big fixes and tweaks this time around like this rumored keyboard enhancement .
The focus will be on making the Liquid Glass user interface more palatable rather than reinventing it or replacing elements.
Expect various usability fixes and more benefits from the revamped Siri, of course.

The event has been trailed with an ‘all systems glow’ tagline – presumably a reference to Apple’s Liquid Glass design language, but it could also be a reference to the way Siri makes the edges of your iPhone glow when activated.

It’s unusual that Apple launches any hardware at this event these days, though it has launched high-end stuff at the event, notably Vision Pro’s first reveal in 2023 or the short-lived iMac Pro in 2017.
In its announcement Apple says: “WWDC26 will spotlight incredible updates for Apple platforms, including AI advancements and exciting new software and developer tools.
As part of the company’s ongoing commitment to supporting developers, WWDC will also provide unique access to Apple engineers and designers, and insight into new tools, frameworks, and features.”

Susan Prescott, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations adds: “WWDC is one of the most exciting times for us at Apple because it’s a chance for our incredible global developer community to come together for an electrifying week that celebrates technology, innovation, and collaboration.”
Apple has had to eat a large amount of humble pie (see the Wall Street Journal interview from YouTube below).
The assistant will be much more conversational , with context-aware, multi-step tasks possible.
And, of course, the benefit is that it will be deeply integrated with your Apple apps and devices in a privacy-first approach.
Plus you can plug other tools such as ChatGPT or Claude into it.

Stuff / Features / What to expect from Apple’s next big event – including new iPhone software and (finally) a revamped Siri
Apple's developer event is next week and not only will there be a updated iOS, but we'll also get the new AI-infused Siri, too

Apple is set to hold its annual developer conference next week and, as always, there will be a lot to talk about, including new software for the iPhone , iPad and Apple Watch. Not only is it CEO Tim Cook’s last outing before he is replaced by John Ternus on 1 September, but it is another big event from Apple’s 50th anniversary year .

In a previous announcement , Apple confirmed WWDC26 (WWDC means Worldwide Developer Conference) will primarily be an online event as it has been for the last few years. But as usual there while there will be a ‘special” in-person part for developers, students and the media on June 8 too. The event has been trailed with an ‘all systems glow’ tagline – presumably a reference to Apple’s Liquid Glass design language, but it could also be a reference to the way Siri makes the edges of your iPhone glow when activated.

You’ll be able to watch the WWDC26 keynote on Apple.com, the Apple Developer app, the Apple Developer website, Apple TV, and YouTube. The likely time for this is 11am PST, 2pm EDT, 6pm GMT, 7pm CEST, 11.30pm IST on 8 June (that’s 2am CST and 4am AEST on 9 June).
Here’s where the keynote video will be on YouTube:

The headline-maker at WWDC26 is likely to be the new AI-infused Siri which is powered by Google Gemini . The announcement of Gemini as a partner was divisive yet understandable so expect Tim Cook and others to underline the privacy of this version of Siri. Indeed, Google might not get much of a mention at all. Expect Apple to be modest about this rather than proclaiming it is the announcement of the decade, largely because Apple Intelligence and the revamped Siri was trailed at WWDC two years ago and the new Siri has been AWOL since then.

Apple has had to eat a large amount of humble pie (see the Wall Street Journal interview from YouTube below). The assistant will be much more conversational , with context-aware, multi-step tasks possible. And, of course, the benefit is that it will be deeply integrated with your Apple apps and devices in a privacy-first approach. Plus you can plug other tools such as ChatGPT or Claude into it. It sounds like there will be a dedicated Siri app to compete with existing AI apps.

As usual we’ll get new software previews for all of Apple’s operating systems, including iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, visionOS 27 and tvOS 27. I presume the naming convention will follow that of last year’s given this is only the second year the new ‘year-by-year’ nomenclature will have been used. As usual, this software will be available for developers straight away, with a public beta to follow at a later date. The final software will then launch in the fall. Expect big fixes and tweaks this time around like this rumored keyboard enhancement . The focus will be on making the Liquid Glass user interface more palatable rather than reinventing it or replacing elements. Expect various usability fixes and more benefits from the revamped Siri, of course. There will also be tweaks to iOS for the upcoming iPhone Fold / iPhone Ultra and explorers will no doubt find some of this in code, even if Apple itself doesn’t talk about it until September.

Possibly. It’s unusual that Apple launches any hardware at this event these days, though it has launched high-end stuff at the event, notably Vision Pro’s first reveal in 2023 or the short-lived iMac Pro in 2017. The Mac Studio wasn’t announced there but it was given a speed boost at the event in 2022 . With the Mac Pro now dead , expect the Mac Studio to receive an M5 Max and M5 Ultra-level upgrade at the event.
It’s unlikely, but there’s still an Apple TV and HomePod mini refresh seemingly in the pipeline and there is a little potential for these to also launch at the event.

In its announcement Apple says: “WWDC26 will spotlight incredible updates for Apple platforms, including AI advancements and exciting new software and developer tools. As part of the company’s ongoing commitment to supporting developers, WWDC will also provide unique access to Apple engineers and designers, and insight into new tools, frameworks, and features.”

Susan Prescott, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations adds: “WWDC is one of the most exciting times for us at Apple because it’s a chance for our incredible global developer community to come together for an electrifying week that celebrates technology, innovation, and collaboration.”

Dan is Editor-in-chief of Stuff, working across the magazine and the Stuff.tv website. Our Editor-in-Chief is a regular at tech shows such as CES in Las Vegas, IFA in Berlin and Mobile World Congress in Barcelona as well as at other launches and events. He has been a CES Innovation Awards judge. Dan is completely platform agnostic and very at home using and writing about Windows, macOS, Android and iOS/iPadOS plus lots and lots of gadgets including audio and smart home gear, laptops and smartphones. He's also been interviewed and quoted in a wide variety of places including The Sun, BBC World Service, BBC News Online, BBC Radio 5Live, BBC Radio 4, Sky News Radio and BBC Local Radio.

passages: John Ternus will become Apple’s new CEO on September 1, replacing Tim Cook after 15 years.
His first major test will come just eight days later, when Apple is expected to unveil its next iPhone generation and potentially its first foldable iPhone.
John Ternus is an engineer who has spent most of his career at Apple.
He joined the company in 2001 and rose through its hardware organisation.
He has worked on major Apple products, including the iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple Watch.
In 2021, he became Apple’s senior vice president of Hardware Engineering.
The iPhone remains central to Apple’s business, but the company needs to find products that can create new growth.
Apple has expanded into services, wearables and mixed-reality hardware, including the Vision Pro.
However, none has yet matched the commercial impact of the iPhone.
That puts greater attention on what comes next.
Before joining Apple, Ternus worked as a mechanical engineer at Virtual Research Systems.
He studied mechanical engineering at the University of Pennsylvania.
His appointment also marks a change in the type of leadership at Apple.
Cook was closely associated with Apple’s operations, supply chain, manufacturing and global business.
Ternus comes from the product and engineering side of the company.
Apple’s board has described Ternus as a leader with deep technical knowledge and a strong focus on product development.
Reports have pointed to a broader product pipeline that could eventually include smart home devices, a tabletop robot, camera-equipped AirPods, smart glasses and other new products.
Apple’s challenge will therefore be bigger than simply producing a foldable handset.
It will need to convince consumers that its approach offers enough value to make the technology mainstream.
The launch could also show whether Ternus intends to push Apple towards more ambitious hardware products.
Apple has confirmed a major product event for September 9.
The event will be the first major Apple launch under Ternus, who will have been CEO for just over a week.
A foldable iPhone is also widely expected, although Apple has not officially confirmed the product.
But hardware alone will not determine his success.
Apple said the CEO transition was part of a long-term succession plan and was unanimously approved by its board.
Cook became Apple CEO in 2011, following the final months of Steve Jobs’ leadership.
During his tenure, Apple expanded its product portfolio and services business while becoming increasingly reliant on a complex global supply chain.
Ternus now inherits that entire operation, but with a different set of challenges.
Artificial intelligence is likely to be one of Ternus’ biggest challenges.
Apple introduced Siri in 2011, but the rise of generative AI has changed the technology landscape.
Companies such as Google, OpenAI and Microsoft have moved quickly with AI assistants, agents and large language models.
Apple, meanwhile, has faced delays in delivering some of its more ambitious Siri upgrades.
The challenge for Ternus is not simply to add more AI features to Apple products.
That matters because Apple’s traditional strength has been the close integration of its hardware, software and services.
At the same time, tensions between the US and China, tariffs, export restrictions and Beijing’s push for domestic technology have created additional risks.
Apple has been expanding production in countries such as India and Vietnam, but moving its entire manufacturing ecosystem away from China is not a simple task.
These specifications remain based on reports and leaks rather than Apple’s official announcement.
If Apple does launch the device, it will enter a category where Samsung and other manufacturers have already spent years developing foldable phones.
That may ultimately be Ternus’ biggest challenge.
The foldable iPhone, if launched as expected, could give Ternus an opportunity to demonstrate that Apple can still enter a new category and influence the market.
Apple also faces a difficult supply-chain challenge.
China remains an important part of Apple’s manufacturing network, with a large ecosystem of suppliers, component makers, skilled workers and production facilities.
If key AI capabilities increasingly come from external companies, Apple could lose some of that control.
The bigger question is: Can Apple build an AI ecosystem that is as influential as the iPhone?
The leadership change comes at a crucial time for Apple.

Ternus comes from the product and engineering side of the company.
Apple’s board has described Ternus as a leader with deep technical knowledge and a strong focus on product development.
Reports have pointed to a broader product pipeline that could eventually include smart home devices, a tabletop robot, camera-equipped AirPods, smart glasses and other new products.
Apple’s challenge will therefore be bigger than simply producing a foldable handset.
It will need to convince consumers that its approach offers enough value to make the technology mainstream.
The launch could also show whether Ternus intends to push Apple towards more ambitious hardware products.
Apple has confirmed a major product event for September 9.
The event will be the first major Apple launch under Ternus, who will have been CEO for just over a week.
A foldable iPhone is also widely expected, although Apple has not officially confirmed the product.
But hardware alone will not determine his success.
Apple said the CEO transition was part of a long-term succession plan and was unanimously approved by its board.
Cook became Apple CEO in 2011, following the final months of Steve Jobs’ leadership.
During his tenure, Apple expanded its product portfolio and services business while becoming increasingly reliant on a complex global supply chain.
Ternus now inherits that entire operation, but with a different set of challenges.
Artificial intelligence is likely to be one of Ternus’ biggest challenges.
Apple introduced Siri in 2011, but the rise of generative AI has changed the technology landscape.
Companies such as Google, OpenAI and Microsoft have moved quickly with AI assistants, agents and large language models.
Apple, meanwhile, has faced delays in delivering some of its more ambitious Siri upgrades.
The challenge for Ternus is not simply to add more AI features to Apple products.
That matters because Apple’s traditional strength has been the close integration of its hardware, software and services.
At the same time, tensions between the US and China, tariffs, export restrictions and Beijing’s push for domestic technology have created additional risks.

That may ultimately be Ternus’ biggest challenge.

Apple also faces a difficult supply-chain challenge.
China remains an important part of Apple’s manufacturing network, with a large ecosystem of suppliers, component makers, skilled workers and production facilities.
If key AI capabilities increasingly come from external companies, Apple could lose some of that control.

The leadership change comes at a crucial time for Apple.
